pages.title: Can I Afford a $25,000 Car?
pages.seoTitle: Can I Afford a $25,000 Car? Salary & Monthly Payment Breakdown
pages.metaDescription: Check if a $25,000 car fits your salary with the 20/4/10 rule. Instant payment, down payment, and transport-budget results—free, no sign up.
pages.intentQuestion: Can I afford a $25,000 car on my salary?
pages.description: Pre-filled $25,000 vehicle affordability check using the 20/4/10 auto rule.

seoContent.intro: This page pre-loads a $25,000 car target with a 20% down payment and 48-month loan so you can instantly see whether the payment fits a 10% transportation budget on your salary.
howToUse: Confirm or edit the $25,000 target price.
Enter your gross annual income.
Adjust down payment %, term, and APR if your quote differs.
Read the live verdict against the 20/4/10 rule.

faqs.question: Can I afford a $25,000 car on my salary?
faqs.answer: Use the 20/4/10 rule: put about 20% down, keep the loan near 4 years, and aim for a payment at or below 10% of gross monthly income. This calculator applies that test to a $25,000 price instantly.

faqs.question: What salary do I need for a $25,000 car?
faqs.answer: After a 20% down payment ($5,000), a typical 48-month loan at mid-single-digit APR often needs roughly $55k–$80k household income to stay near the 10% transport cap—adjust rate and insurance in the inputs for your quote.

faqs.question: Is the 20/4/10 rule required by lenders?
faqs.answer: No. It is a consumer planning heuristic. Lenders use credit, DTI, and residual value rules. 20/4/10 is intentionally stricter than many approvals.

pages.title: Can I Afford a $500,000 House?
pages.seoTitle: Can I Afford a $500,000 House? 28/36 DTI & Payment Breakdown
pages.metaDescription: See if a $500,000 home fits your income with the 28/36 DTI rule. Instant PITI estimate, free online, no sign up.
pages.description: Pre-filled $500,000 home purchase check using 28/36 debt-to-income guidelines.

seoContent.intro: A $500,000 purchase price is pre-loaded with 20% down and a 30-year mortgage so you can stress-test the payment against the 28/36 DTI rule before you tour homes.
howToUse: Keep or edit the $500,000 target price.
Enter household gross income and existing monthly debts.
Set taxes/insurance escrow for your ZIP.
Compare housing and total DTI caps in the live results.

faqs.question: Can I afford a $500,000 house?
faqs.answer: Under the 28/36 rule, housing (PITI) should stay near 28% of gross income and all debts under 36%. This page models a $500,000 price with your income, rate, and down payment.

faqs.question: What income do I need for a $500k home?
faqs.answer: With 20% down, a mid-6% rate, and typical taxes/insurance, many households need roughly $110k–$140k gross to stay near 28% housing DTI—run your exact numbers above.

faqs.question: Does 28/36 include utilities?
faqs.answer: Standard DTI focuses on PITI and contractual debts, not utilities or groceries. Still budget those separately so the leftover is realistic.

pages.title: Can I Afford a $30,000 Wedding?
pages.seoTitle: Can I Afford a $30,000 Wedding? Cash Cushion & Savings Plan
pages.metaDescription: Plan a $30,000 wedding without wrecking your emergency fund. 50/30/20 and cash-cushion check—free calculator, no sign up.
pages.description: Pre-filled $30,000 wedding cost check with cash cushion and savings timeline.

seoContent.intro: Weddings are one-time lifestyle purchases. This engine checks whether a $30,000 celebration can be funded without wiping a 3-month expense cushion—and how long a savings plan would take.
howToUse: Confirm the $30,000 wedding target.
Enter cash on hand and essential monthly expenses.
Set a realistic monthly savings contribution.
Review the cash-cushion and months-to-save results.

faqs.question: Can I afford a $30,000 wedding?
faqs.answer: Yes if you can pay (or finish saving) without dropping below ~3 months of essential expenses, and the monthly savings fit inside a healthy wants allocation under 50/30/20.

faqs.question: Should I finance a wedding on credit cards?
faqs.answer: Usually no. High-APR wedding debt often fails both the cash-cushion and debt-payoff tests. Prefer a shorter savings timeline or a smaller celebration.

faqs.question: How does 50/30/20 apply to weddings?
faqs.answer: Treat contributions as wants (30%) or as a dedicated savings goal (20% bucket) until the date—not as needs unless you are covering mandatory deposits already owed.

pages.title: Can I Afford a New iPhone?
pages.seoTitle: Can I Afford a New iPhone? Cash Cushion Purchase Check
pages.metaDescription: See if a new iPhone fits your cash cushion and 50/30/20 wants budget. Free instant check, no sign up.
pages.h1: Can I Afford a New iPhone?
pages.intentQuestion: Can I afford a new iPhone?
pages.description: Pre-filled flagship phone purchase (~$1,200) with emergency-fund protection check.

seoContent.intro: Flagship phones feel small next to a house payment—but they still fail the cash-cushion test when the emergency fund is thin. This page starts at a typical ~$1,200 unlocked iPhone price.
howToUse: Set the phone (or storage/config) price.
Enter cash on hand and monthly essentials.
See whether buying now protects a 3-month cushion.
Or read how many months of saving close the gap.

faqs.question: Can I afford a new iPhone?
faqs.answer: If cash covers the price and you still keep ~3 months of expenses in reserve, yes. If not, save inside your 30% wants budget or choose a lower storage tier / certified refurbished model.

faqs.question: Is carrier financing a good idea?
faqs.answer: 0% financing can be fine if you already budget the payment as a want and keep your emergency fund intact. High-APR retail financing usually fails this engine’s cushion check.

faqs.question: What rule applies to gadgets?
faqs.answer: Use a cash-cushion check plus 50/30/20 wants capacity—not mortgage-style DTI. Gadgets are discretionary purchases.

pages.title: Can I Afford a Gym Membership?
pages.seoTitle: Can I Afford a Gym Membership? 50/30/20 Monthly Cost Check
pages.metaDescription: Check whether a gym membership fits your 30% wants budget. Instant 50/30/20 lifestyle calculator—free, no sign up.
pages.h1: Can I Afford a Gym Membership?
pages.intentQuestion: Can I afford a gym membership?
pages.description: Pre-filled ~$55/mo gym membership check against the 50/30/20 wants slice.

seoContent.intro: Subscriptions stack quietly. This page tests a typical gym dues amount against your 30% wants allocation after other discretionary spending.
howToUse: Enter your monthly gym (or studio) price.
Add other wants: streaming, dining out, hobbies.
Compare the total to 30% of gross monthly income.
Adjust income or cut other wants if you are over the cap.

faqs.question: Can I afford a gym membership?
faqs.answer: If gym dues plus your other wants stay inside ~30% of income (50/30/20), the membership is usually affordable. Annualize the cost to see the true yearly hit.

faqs.question: What about personal trainers?
faqs.answer: Trainer sessions are still wants. Add them into Other Wants / Mo or raise Gym Cost to the all-in monthly wellness total.

faqs.question: Is gross or net income better for 50/30/20?
faqs.answer: Purists use after-tax income. This tool uses gross for fast comparison with other CalculioHub affordability pages—tighten the cap if your tax rate is high.

seoContent.intro: The master affordability calculator accepts any target. Leave “recurring” off for one-time purchases (cash cushion + savings plan) or turn it on to test a monthly habit against 50/30/20 wants.
howToUse: Enter the price (one-time) or monthly cost (recurring).
Toggle recurring if this is a subscription or lifestyle habit.
Fill income, cash, expenses, and other wants.
Read the verdict and adjust until the plan feels safe.

faqs.question: Can I afford this purchase or monthly cost?
faqs.answer: For one-time buys, protect a 3-month expense cushion. For recurring costs, keep wants near 30% of income. This master tool runs both modes with the same Affordability Engine.

faqs.question: How is this different from the category pages?
faqs.answer: Category pages pre-fill intent targets ($25k car, $500k house, iPhone, gym, wedding). This page is the blank interactive calculator for anything else.

faqs.question: Are these results a loan approval?
faqs.answer: No. CalculioHub provides planning estimates only. Lenders use credit scores, verified income, and underwriting guidelines.
